title: Man and van: what to expect
summary: What to include in your request, what providers may ask, and how to compare the responses you receive.
imageAlt: A mover securing household items inside a panel van

sections.heading: Start with a useful description
paragraphs: A man-and-van request works best when the provider can picture the job before getting in touch. Include the collection and delivery areas, your preferred date, the main items, the number of stairs and whether either property has awkward access.
Photos and rough measurements are especially helpful for bulky furniture. Mention anything unusually heavy, fragile or difficult to dismantle rather than leaving it as a moving-day surprise.
checklist: Preferred date or flexible date range
Stairs, lifts, parking and access restrictions

sections.heading: Expect a few practical questions
paragraphs: Your request is reviewed before it can be shared with suitable providers. An available operator may then contact you to clarify the load, timing, access or the amount of lifting help required. That conversation is the right time to confirm what is included and whether the job sounds realistic for the proposed van and crew.

sections.heading: Compare the whole response
paragraphs: Price matters, but it is not the only useful detail. Compare the proposed vehicle, number of helpers, estimated time, availability and any conditions the provider has explained. Public profiles may also show verification and reviews where that information has been published.
A response is not a confirmed booking by itself. Make sure you and the provider agree the final scope, timing, payment arrangements and contact details directly before moving day.

sections.heading: Make the handover easy
paragraphs: Have everything packed and ready unless packing help was specifically agreed. Keep keys, documents, medicines and high-value personal items with you, and point out fragile pieces before loading begins. A clear inventory and reachable phone number help the day start without avoidable delays.

sections.heading: Questions worth settling before the day
paragraphs: Ask who will arrive, what vehicle they plan to use and how they would like changes to the inventory reported. Confirm the arrival window, addresses and the best number to call if access or timing changes. If you need help dismantling or reassembling furniture, say so explicitly rather than assuming it is part of the service.

It is also useful to understand how the provider handles waiting time, extra items and delays outside either party's control. Clear answers protect both sides from different expectations. Keep the agreed details somewhere you can reach on moving day, along with any parking instructions or building contact information.

title: How to prepare for moving day
summary: A straightforward checklist for packing, access, parking and the final hour before the van arrives.
imageAlt: Packed moving boxes and furniture ready beside a front door

sections.heading: Confirm what is actually moving
paragraphs: Walk through every room and make one list of the items going in the van. Include cupboards, lofts, sheds and anything waiting outside. If the load has changed since your first request, tell the provider before the day so they can check that the vehicle, time and number of helpers still make sense.
checklist: Photos of bulky or fragile pieces

sections.heading: Pack for carrying, not just storage
paragraphs: Use boxes that can close securely and avoid making any one box too heavy to lift safely. Fill empty spaces so contents do not move around, protect sharp corners and label fragile boxes clearly. Keep fixings from dismantled furniture together in a named bag rather than loose in a drawer.
Set aside a small essentials bag with keys, chargers, drinks, basic cleaning supplies and anything you will need before the rest is unpacked.

sections.heading: Plan the route from door to van
paragraphs: Check parking at both addresses, including permits, loading restrictions and building rules. Clear hallways, prop internal doors safely where appropriate and protect any surface that needs extra care. If there is a lift, confirm its operating hours and whether it must be reserved.
Let the provider know about long carries, narrow staircases or entrances that are difficult to reach. Access can affect the time and equipment needed just as much as the distance between addresses.

sections.heading: Do one final check
paragraphs: Before the van leaves, check each room and compare the load with your list. Keep important documents and valuables with you, confirm the destination contact can be reached, and make sure everyone understands where the van is heading next.

sections.heading: Leave room for the unexpected
paragraphs: Moving days rarely run to the minute. Build a little flexibility around key collection, lift access and travel, and avoid arranging another time-sensitive appointment immediately after the expected finish. Charge your phone and share any important updates with the provider as soon as they happen.

At the destination, decide roughly where the larger items should go before unloading starts. Simple room labels can reduce repeated lifting and keep entrances clearer. Once the van is empty, check it with the provider, compare the delivered items with your list and report any concern promptly while the details are still fresh.

title: What size van do you need?
summary: How to describe your load accurately so an operator can recommend a suitable vehicle and crew.
imageAlt: A mover measuring furniture beside an open medium panel van

sections.heading: Describe the load, not the room count
paragraphs: Two studio flats can contain very different amounts of furniture, so room count is only a starting point. List the largest items first, then estimate the number of boxes, bags and smaller pieces. Photos give a provider a much clearer sense of shape and volume than labels such as small or medium move.

sections.heading: Think about shape as well as volume
paragraphs: A long sofa, tall wardrobe or large mattress can determine the vehicle needed even when the rest of the load is light. Tell the provider which pieces come apart and measure doorways if access looks tight. Loose bags and open containers are harder to stack securely than closed boxes.

sections.heading: The crew matters too
paragraphs: Van size and lifting help are separate decisions. A suitable vehicle does not remove the need for enough people to handle stairs, bulky furniture or a long carry. Be clear about whether you can help and whether another person will be available at either end.

If timing is important, mention it early. A larger vehicle may reduce repeat journeys, while extra help may make loading and unloading more practical. The provider can explain the setup they believe fits the job.

sections.heading: Let the operator confirm the fit
paragraphs: Avoid choosing a vehicle from a generic capacity chart alone. Vehicle interiors and load shapes vary, and safe loading needs usable space around the items. Share your inventory, measurements and photos, then ask the operator to confirm their proposed van before you agree the job.

sections.heading: Recheck when the inventory changes
paragraphs: A few late additions can make a bigger difference than they appear to. Garden furniture, bicycles, plants, mirrors and loose bags often occupy awkward gaps and may not stack like uniform boxes. If you sell, add or replace a large item after the first conversation, send an updated list or photo rather than waiting until collection.

The same applies when furniture cannot be dismantled as expected. Tell the operator which measurements changed and let them decide whether the original plan still works. A timely update may prevent a second journey, a vehicle change or an avoidable delay at the kerb, especially when access or parking time is limited.
